chapter: Teddy Wilson, Cafe Society and bebop
title: Feeling lost as a soloist among Carl George, Harold Baker and Buck Clayton
summary: He admired the new trumpet styles but could not play the Kansas City blues style, and felt finished as a soloist in the Wilson band.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Now, this is now 1939, you were listening to people like Louie Armstrong and Freddie Keppard?
Who were you listening to by 1939, what trumpet players were you --
Well, naturally, I was in the band with Carl George. And Harold Baker, and they were entirely new, their style of playing was entirely new to me. And I liked it very much --

-- and I felt absolutely lost, as a soloist because to get up there and play New Orleans style of solo in that band, would be -- have been out of place, entirely out of place and it wouldn't have fitted in there in the first place. It would've been entirely out of place. But you see there were a lot of other trumpet -- but New York you had other trumpet players that, you know, you were listening to at different times, like Buck Clayton.
Who was doing a lot of recording.
And that was also a different style from New Orleans.
I liked it, but I couldn't play it. I couldn't play the Kansas City style.
Of course, you know, we didn't do a lot of blues work in Chicago. That was mostly, what they call now, Dixieland music.
So Basie's band was built mostly around -- styled around Blues. And I wasn't too familiar with that.

And it bothered me a lot and then Harold Baker playing another different beautiful style. And Carl George, and I was just confused, I couldn't get together, I couldn't -- I didn't know what to do. So I was just there, I was just a member of the band. That's all they kept me in the band. But I was -- as a soloist I was out, finished.
